newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends lower on profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends lower on profit-taking.

text.p: NEW YORK, April 15 - The dollar fell against the German mark on Tuesday after profit-taking wiped out early gains that were sparked by remarks by a senior German central bank official and a rally in stocks and bonds.
Currency traders also continued to weigh the possibility of central bank intervention to boost the yen, a concern that kept the dollar from making further gains against the Japanese currency.

Ben Strauss, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Bank Julius Baer and Co. in New York, described the dollar's retreat as "just an accumulation of profit-takers, nothing really out of the ordinary."

German Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing said the launch of the single European currency, or euro, could cause shifts from investments denominated in marks into dollar-denominated investments. He spoke at a conference in Frankfurt, Germany, on European Economic and Monetary Union, which is scheduled to began on Jan. 1, 1999.

"I think it implies that we should see the dollar continue to be strong for some time until EMU either falls apart or gets solid enough for people to reinvest in those areas," said Elliott Dix, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Signet Bank.
Shortly after Issing's comments reached currency markets, the dollar surged briefly to 1.7375 marks, its highest level in more than three years.
Adding to the dollar's upward momentum was a rally in U.S. stock and bond markets following news that inflationary pressures were surprisingly tame in March.

A Labour Department report showing a modest increase in the consumer price index for March boosted the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond a full point and sent the Dow Jones industrial average saoring. The Dow initially rose about 80 points, then dipped before roaring back in late trading to finish more than 135 points higher at 6,587.
"The stock and bond markets both up today did not hurt at all," said Frank Pusateri at Mellon Bank in Boston.

He hesitated to draw a direct correlation between the initial rise in the dollar and gains in stock and bond prices. "But certainly from a psychological level, it certainly gave a lot of confidence to the move already under way," he said.
The move higher began to unravel by midday as some traders sold dollars.
In late New York trading, the dollar settled at 1.7270 marks, down from 1.7310 marks on Monday. The dollar fell to 126.07 yen from 126.63 yen.

Throughout the session, the dollar failed to make much headway against the Japanese currency. Traders pointed to profit-taking and fears that Japan's central bank might step into the market to stop the yen's fall.

Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka recently vowed to act decisively against excessive movements in the currency market but avoided the question of what exchange rate would trigger intervention on behalf of the yen.

Central bank intervention is definitely on the minds of traders but this will probably not happen until the dollar rises too fast toward 130 yen, said Doug Lee, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Sakura Bank Ltd. in New York.
In other trading, the dollar slid to 1.4670 Swiss francs from 1.4725 francs, and to Canadian $1.3970 from C$1.3995. The British pound climbed to $1.6288 from $1.6205.
